172.t: Trombone novelty pieces and band repertoire
172.s: Slim Trombone and sliding trombone pieces, and tunes the band played.
172.q: I played Slim Trombone, I think. I never really had a solid trombone. We played sliding jim and various other things we used to make ourselves, you know, at that time. We'd done more sliding than anything else, you see, because that's what made the hit at that time. We played the side somewhere.

172.t: Zue Robertson, Roy Palmer and George Filhe
172.s: Russell asks about trombonists he knew elsewhere; Ridgley comments.
172.ch: Trombonists, Tiger Rag and carnival work
172.q: Real good. I never got to know him. I never heard him. I think when he left, I think he got on police force in Chicago. I think he got to be a detective. Him, a Tucker, he was one of us. I think George Field. I was a Tucker. I think I got on police force. He got to be a detective.

172.t: Favorite old trombonists and Jack Carey
172.s: Ridgley loved Big Jasper and Jack Carey, who played by ear.
172.ch: Trombonists, Tiger Rag and carnival work
172.q: Well, I'll tell you, I used to love the old man Big Jasper. He was nice on trombone. Smooth, I played. But there was a further noise there. It was all the light, you see. So you'd get a kink out of them and see they could raise so much playing on that trombone. They'd give you a good time. You were…

172.t: Importance of the trombone and the bag of tricks
172.s: Dutcher calls the trombone the hardest part. Ridgley says players like Frankie Dusen made good parts without reading and everyone kept a stock of licks, always staying in the chord and finding the melody on piano.
172.q: But you know those trombone players. Like Franky Dusen, he could make good parts from ones and he couldn't read nothing harder. But he could make good parts.

172.s: Ridgley recalls George Fields as the first trombone player he knew, playing in the district, and says Tucker was earlier.
172.q: That's the man that I was trying to get to hear about. George Field. That's the man. That's the first trombone player, George Field. I'll say to you something else.

172.t: Eddie Atkins, Zue Robertson and Roy Palmer
172.s: Ridgley recalls Atkins with Joe Oliver, Zue Robertson taught by Batiste, and Roy Palmer in the Tuxedo brass band.
172.q: Somewhere. Eddie was a good trombone player. He's buried in the same graveyard as Joe Avery. At that time him and Nora and this other boy, he died, or he must have died with. Now he was a good trombone, Zoo. Zoo? Yeah. Zoo Robertson? Yeah. He was a good trombone player. Who did he work with? He was…

172.t: Roy Palmer's fast execution and Jack Carey
172.s: They discuss Roy Palmer working in a steel mill, how he compares for speed to earlier players, and Jack Carey; Ridgley says he always stayed in New Orleans apart from boat trips.
172.q: You've got them. I forgot all about them. Just like they think about me, I think some of them did. They think the same thing about me. They haven't wait for me for so long.

172.t: Trombone players Carnish, Dusen, Sonny Henry and others
172.s: Assessments of New Orleans trombonists, some readers and some by ear.
172.ch: Trombonists, Tiger Rag and carnival work
172.q: No. But he had a good ear. See? He played mostly by the... Frankie Duesen wasn't a good reader. But he had a good ear. See? Poor ear. At the time he was... He wasn't a good reader. But I believe he picked up there. I think he reads pretty well now, they say. I believe.

172.t: Dutcher asks how Dixieland trombone is played; most played by ear
172.s: Dutcher asks what a trombonist thinks about when improvising. Ridgley says old trombonists were mostly a gift and played by ear, naming those who could and could not read.
172.ch: Faking parts and the Tuxedo bands
172.q: Well, at our time back there, you know, we wasn't much of a reader. Spellers, and the trombone, he didn't do much. Most of the time he had bass licks, you know. And then he had nod, then he'd have a little solo or something. But he didn't play trombone like those fellas. The most was a gift, and we…

172.s: Discussion of how high a trombone can go (B-flat, F). Ridgley says Nora Dutrey and Eddie Atkins could go higher and Ory was not too high.
172.q: Oh, so, Nora Dutre and Eddie Atkin, they could go above that. They was high, man. They could hit F probably. I don't know what it was hit up there, but they could go higher than that. Nobody ever hits a B-flat above that B-flat. No, not that B-flat. No, no, no. So, it's only one B-flat that we can…

172.s: Trombonist who spent years in Jacksonville and came back to play again; the talk drifts to wives who stayed away.
172.q: But this is what happened to him. He uh, went out of the audible mile. Oh I believe I heard that. And he stayed in Jacksonville about 14 or 15 years.

172.t: How high and low the trombone played
172.s: Dutcher asks what share of the notes were above or below F. Ridgley says about half, and he preferred playing higher near the trumpet rather than imitating a bass.
172.q: I don't know, bass is the full line. I mean? Bass chord, F. F is the full line. I'd be… Well, I'm thinking of the bass… Yeah, that's right.

172.t: Trombone as humming bass part and trombone taking the lead
172.s: Ridgley describes the trombone as a humming bass part with solo licks, and says the trombone could take the lead early on.
172.q: We never did have a night at the trombone. Someone would be playing like that in dancing music. We'd learn as to bump and bump, bump, like a ba, a solo ba, ba, and so on. Until we used to rip and slide and get all that. But we used to get along. We used to like it.

172.t: Ridgley on how much he has forgotten
172.s: Ridgley says he has forgotten many things and describes his bass-singing trombone style. He says musicians then knew less theory than today's.
172.q: See, this was just so many things that I did at the time, you know. Well, of course, it's gone from the night. Sure. See, but I could do plenty of things. You know, when it came in, it would be late, and I could just grab up some time and make my different part in it that I never had been making. I…

172.t: Changing from bass violin to slide trombone
172.s: He moved from bass violin to slide trombone at Welch's urging because it was more exciting; talk of bass parts.
172.q: We were, I was with several lead bands when I was trading from trombone, bass violin to trombone. See, we had the old man who was a key trombone player, you know. But in the beginning, when he came in the band, but after he was with us a while, he went back to the bass violin, you see, then he took…

70.t: Jimmy Harrison's swing trombone and those who copied him
70.s: Jackson calls Harrison the greatest swing trombonist he heard, with Sandy Williams and Jack Teagarden borrowing from him.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: -- he and Claude Jones. Jimmy Harrison at that time was the greatest swing trombone player that I ever heard. He could do more with five notes. He could play five notes and use them so they would swing you to death and then still be interesting, you see.

70.t: Dickie Wells, who almost talked on the trombone
70.s: Wells came through Springfield with Cecil Scott, later played with Teddy Hill and Basie, and kidded Vic Dickinson.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Dickie Wells came through my home with Cecil Scott. I thought he was the most phenomenal trombone player I had ever heard. He was making a lot of glisses and he was -- he could almost do a conversation with the horn. Then later on when I heard him, he had left Cecil and he went with Teddy Hill.…

70.t: Lawrence Brown's soft playing and Duke taking him for three trombones
70.s: Brown strolled between tables playing quietly; McKinney would not hire him, so when Redman had three trombones Duke grabbed Brown.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Yeah. I never heard nothing that fast. I never heard a trombone player like that, not like Lawrence was playing in those days. Now, when I met him in Sebastian's Cotton Club, he was working with Les Hite. Now, in between dance sets of the show, there was a piano player named Harvey Brooks and…

70.t: J. J. Johnson as the revolutionary modern trombonist
70.s: Asked who did for trombone what Blanton did for bass, Jackson names J. J. Johnson, whom he first heard in Benny Carter's band at the Apollo.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Oh, God. It was in the forties, if I'm not mistaken. It was in the forties. Bennie Carter brought a band to the Apollo Theater.

70.t: Carl Fontana, Frank Rosolino and Urbie Green
70.s: He names Carl Fontana and Frank Rosolino as favorites, and calls Urbie Green the greatest all-around trombonist.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Oh, I don't even mention Urbie Herbie. I don't mention him because to me Urbie Herbie is the tops over everything.

70.s: Big George Matthews played melodic trombone, was still active, and played in the Apollo band under Reuben Phillips.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: But the brass section always astounded me. Oh, big George Matthews was one of the trombone players, I think, in there, too, for a while.

70.t: Trombonists and bassists stay close; Tony Studd and George Roberts
70.s: Jackson says trombone and bass players love each other; Tony Studd taught him embouchure and attack, and George Roberts is his favorite bass trombonist.
70.q: Uh-huh. Well, do you know, to me there's two instruments in the band that they always seem to be close to one another. Trombone players have always been close to one another and so have bass players.

70.t: Jimmy Harrison, the trombonist who influenced others
70.s: Jackson names Harrison first among trombone influences, saying many stole from him including Benny Morton and Teagarden.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: a great swing trombone player. He would make you pat your foot. There was a lot of guys that, I think, stole from him. I have to say they stole from him.

70.t: Bill Watrous and Jackson's reputation as super sideman
70.s: Jackson praises Bill Watrous, who calls him father and practices hours daily; Hinton says trombonists credit Jackson's influence.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: And we got another young trombone player that's coming up today, to me, that is right -- he's right on the verge, and that's Bill Watrous.

70.t: White trombonists: Miff Mole, Tommy Dorsey, Jack Jenney, Will Bradley, Buddy Morrow
70.s: Jackson recalls white trombonists he heard, from Miff Mole through Billy Rausch and Jack Jenney across from Redman's band, to Buddy Morrow the iron man.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: We haven't mentioned Tommy, we haven't mentioned Jack Janney. [handwritten correction: 'Janney' struck through, 'Jenney' written above]

70.s: Asked who most impressed him, Jackson declines to name a greatest, crediting Claude Jones for starting him and something from each of the others.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Now, you know, I got so much from each one of them individually that when you go to say, 'Now, who influenced you the most,' -- Of course, Claude Jones was really the cause of

70.t: Claude Jones as his inspiration, and Lawrence Brown's later influence
70.s: Claude Jones talked him into trombone and was his model; Dickie Wells seemed too complicated, and Lawrence Brown influenced everyone after 1932.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: He talked me into, really talked me into playing trombone. I didn't have no idea of ever playing a trombone before, and if you listen to Claude Jones anyway, Claude Jones could talk you into anything, if you knew Claude, --

70.s: Trummy Young was noticed with Lunceford and Louis Armstrong but preferred Hawaii; Eddie Bert is a friend of Trummy's.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: Trummy Young, the only reason that he didn't get to stay on the New York scene too much because he wanted to live in Hawaii. He left this country to go to Hawaii and live. He had his own band in Hawaii in a hotel there. And he left to come out with Louie.

70.t: DePriest Wheeler and the bass trombone
70.s: Jackson never saw Wheeler's bass trombone, having only subbed in his place and joined after Wheeler left.
70.ch: Musicians of the era: players, drummers, bassists, pianists
70.q: I never saw it. Because the first bass trombone player I ever saw in a jazz band was with Stan Kenton. That was the first one I saw.

418.t: Good lead trombonists he knew, including Dan Minor and Dickie Wells
418.s: He declines to name the best lead trombonist but recalls Dan Minor, Dickie Wells and Henry Coker from the Basie band.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: Oh, that would be hard to say. That would really be hard to say. I don't know. I don't want to do anybody any injustice. That's why I wouldn't say.

418.t: Good lead trombonists he knew, including Dan Minor and Dickie Wells
418.s: He declines to name the best lead trombonist but recalls Dan Minor, Dickie Wells and Henry Coker.
418.ch: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
418.q: Oh, that would be hard to say. That would really be hard to say. I don't know. I don't want to do anybody any injustice. That's why I wouldn't say it.

418.t: Good lead trombonists he knew, including Dan Minor and Dickie Wells
418.s: He declines to name the best lead trombonist but recalls Dan Minor, Dickie Wells and Henry Coker.
418.ch: Technique and life on the road (repeated passages)
418.q: Oh, that would be hard to say. That would really be hard to say. I don't know. I don't want to do anybody any injustice. That's why I wouldn't say.

418.t: Ballad playing on trombone and Goodbye Rose
418.s: Ballad trombone existed early; he remembers a beautiful trombone solo on Goodbye Rose played by a man he cannot name.
418.q: Sure. Yeah. I remember a long while ago, a trombone player -- I don't remember who he was -- but there was a piece called 'Goodbye Rose.' And it was just a beautiful trombone solo this guy played.

418.t: Ballad playing on trombone and Goodbye Rose
418.s: Ballad trombone existed early; he remembers a beautiful trombone solo on Goodbye Rose by a man he cannot name.
418.q: Sure. Yes. I remember a long while ago, a trombone player, I don't remember who he was... There was a piece called "Goodbye, Rose." And it was just a beautiful trombone solo this guy played.

418.t: Ballad playing on trombone and Goodbye Rose
418.s: Ballad trombone existed early; he remembers a beautiful trombone solo on Goodbye Rose by a man he cannot name.
418.q: Sure. Yeah. I remember a long while ago, a trombone player -- I don't remember who he was -- but there was a piece called 'Goodbye Rose.' And it was just a beautiful trombone solo this guy played.

418.t: An old trombone ballad record and the circus-instrument myth
418.s: They listen to a c. 1910 record with a remarkable trombone ballad solo, and Morgenstern says it is wrong that the trombone was a circus instrument before jazz players got hold of it.
418.ch: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
418.q: That's what I've been trying to tell you. The guys have been playing that for years -- music like that.

259.t: Favorite trombonists and Kit Harris's band
259.s: He names early trombone players, then Louie and George Nelson, who played with Kit Harris's band with George Williams and bassist Richard McLean.
259.q: He said, who was your favorite trombone player way back in those days? Who was the? Your favorite trombone player. Who was the best one? Yeah, your favorite. Oh, you know, I see. I left before I could play music good. It's, uh, let me see. Rob Palmer, did you say you know him? He's living there,…

259.t: Robichaux trombonists: Vic Gasper and Johnny Lindsey
259.s: Names the Robichaux trombone players and clears up Johnny versus Joe Lindsey, who played with Pierron.
259.q: Who was a trombone player with Robo Show? Who was a trombone player? Oak Gasper. Not Oak. No, Oak's brother. What's his name? Victor. Yeah, Vic Gasper. He was a trombone player. Johnny, Johnny, Johnny, Johnny, Johnny, Johnny should play trombone with him too.

259.t: Frankie Dusen's band and Joe Howard
259.s: He recalls Frankie Dusen's band with trumpeter Joe Howard, who later played tuba, and where Dusen lived and what he played.
259.q: Huh? Who was in his band? Uh, let me see, uh, the trumpet player was, uh, I know you know him, uh, what do you call this man? I don't know much about Franky Dusen. I don't know much about Franky Dusen. There he is. He never had my tongue, I think.

259.t: Vermilla and Joe Johnson the trombonist
259.s: He does not know Vermilla; the interviewers identify a trombonist, Joe Johnson, from Algiers who worked with him.
259.q: Who is Vermilla? Vermilla. Vermilla? Yeah. I don't think I know him. He said you talk about him once. I don't know him. I don't know him. Vermilla.

259.t: Trombonist Eddie Vincent, who shares his name
259.s: Asked about Eddie Vinson, Vincent says he met him in Chicago, noted that they share a name, and could not place him otherwise.
259.ch: Banjo career, Armstrong and the Liberty Bell
259.q: So did you know Eddie Vinson? Who? Eddie Vinson. Eddie? Eddie Vinson. Eddie Vinson. Eddie Vinson. He's a trombone. Same name with me. Yeah, a trombone player. So did you know him? No, I don't know him. You didn't know Eddie Vinson? No. I know him. Eddie Vinson. The same name with my last name,…

259.s: Vincent comes up with Robert Thomas, a trombonist now sick.
259.q: You work with Bob Thomas in it? Who? Bob Thomas. Robert Thomas. Palmer? Oh, Palmer. No, Thomas. Thomas Thomas. Robert Thomas.

18.s: He met trombonist Jimmy Harrison in 1928, loved his comedy and music, and describes his slurred, low-technique style.
18.ch: Family, Margaret's story and Eutris's memories
18.q: Doodle-e-doo-e-doo-e-doo (HUMS) - that's what you hear on every one of his records. He didn't use much tongue. JCH: Slur, that's exactly what he did. He slurred a lot... While the other band was playing we used to sit at a table and tell jokes... and he'd

18.t: Benny Morton's growl versus J. J. Johnson's technique
18.s: He calls Morton's growl part of his tone but J. J. just a technician where everything goes by.
18.ch: Family lore, Boston and Europe with Sam Price
18.q: I haven't heard anybody with the style of Benny Morton, because most of the time when he plays, he growls, but not like Tricky Sam growled. That was part of his tone; that's the way he played. But Jay Jay Johnson, that was nothing but just technician, everything is going-going-going-going, and you…

18.t: Cricket on his father's place in history
18.s: He says his father was the best lip-slur trombonist, that Teagarden was overrated.
18.ch: Favorite bands, advice and family reflections
18.q: I don't know very much technically about the trombone playing but he tells me that before J. J. Johnson, that is, youknow during my father's time, there was a style of playing where they used a lot of lip slurs and now it's mostly through counting and staccato with the trombone where it used to be…

18.t: Kid Ory and not copying anyone
18.s: He last played with Ory and Teagarden at Newport; he insists he never copied any trombonist.
18.ch: Early influences, Oliver date and trombone peers
18.q: No, I don't want to make no kind of remark one way or the other. No, I just know he was one of these old-time trombone players, not playing a whole lot of jazz notes, doin' the less slide.

18.t: Trummy Young and the Denmark record
18.s: Trummy Young copies him note for note; in Denmark a patron played him a record of I'm Confessing.
18.ch: Early influences, Oliver date and trombone peers
18.q: I'd be glad to say it, Trummy Young. Note for note. He came and told me, he said, "I'm going to steal every thing that I can from you." And I said, "Thank you." It made me work harder. I have a record I made back there over in Denmark and the guy, I have his picture there, he sent for me. He owned…

18.s: He recalls trumpeter Ed Swayzee of Arkansas and touring together with a show.
18.ch: Early influences, Oliver date and trombone peers
18.q: He's from Arkansas. That's a little bit before your time. Someone was asking me about him not so long ago.

257.t: Trombone gigs hard to get; J.J. Johnson and Fed Terrell
257.s: Trombone was hard to book when he was coming up, so he doubled on piano; he recalls replacing J.J. Johnson in a Fed Terrell band and trombone's rise in rock and roll.
257.ch: Career, brass bands and choice of instrument
257.q: But you know at one time, I mean during the time I was coming up, you know it was pretty hard for Trumont Player to get a job, you know. And if I wouldn't have went with Joe Robichill, Clement and I, we wouldn't, I guess probably wouldn't be playing that music. Mm-hmm.

257.t: Boots, the smooth trombonist turned bassist
257.s: Joseph praises Boots as a fine, smooth trombonist who played melody, used to fetch him for jobs, and helped him; Russell only heard him on bass.
257.q: have studied? Well, as a fellow, there's something else I forgot to tell you too. I think he was a great trombone player, but people never talked about him. He was smooth, and he was a fellow who gave me an idea of, you know, peeing up on your ground and playing melody too, was Boots.

257.t: Other trombonists he admired: Teagarden, Vic Gaspar
257.s: He always liked Jack Teagarden but never heard him locally, and never heard older players such as Vic Gaspar.
257.q: See like Vic Gaspar and a lot of those fellas, I never did a chance to really hear him or proud of him or proud of him I didn't even know them.

257.s: Russell asks about valve trombonists such as Frankie Dusen and Morris French; Joseph never heard them.
257.ch: New Orleans trombone style and composing
257.q: That's Albert French uncle, no? Yes. No, Bill, I never heard.

257.t: Ory's Creole Trombone at Mardi Gras
257.s: With Paul he plays Ory's Creole Trombone on the street; he bought the music, never saw Ory, and Russell recalls interviewing him in California.
257.ch: New Orleans trombone style and composing
257.q: Well I don't have too many of them. About two or three of them. And I got the other two I have in mind I don't have no title for them. Mm-hmm. Now Paul and I got to get on the slide for a slide because when I got with them at the Mardi Gras a lot of people used to ask for

227.t: Great trombonists: Harris, Nanton, Jenney, Teagarden
227.s: Mandel surveys trombone voices from Bill Harris and Lawrence Brown to Tricky Sam Nanton, Jack Jenney, Teagarden and Tommy Dorsey.
227.ch: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
227.q: He’s another one-of-a-kind, he was incredible, and he was the guy I was listening to before Earl Swope took my head off. So it was great hearing them in, The Second Herd, together, ‘cause they loved each other. Bill Harris, nobody ever played like him, before or since, but he was different, he was…

227.t: Playing lead trombone and Ginnie Powell
227.s: Mandel says he followed Trummy Young and Tommy Pederson as lead trombonist in Raeburn's band on high chops, and mentions singer Ginnie Powell.
227.q: It sure is and Tommy Pederson before that. I couldn’t play like that, you know I really wasn’t that good, but for some reason I fitted.

227.t: The Jimmy Dorsey trombone book and Bobby Byrne
227.s: Mandel describes the trombone chair in Jimmy Dorsey's band, written for Tommy-style players, and following Bobby Byrne and Moe Zudekoff.
227.ch: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
227.q: That’s right, he did and he was a good trombone player, but he was kind of, sort of like Tommy in that way, you know he was a very good smooth trombone player. Very good musician.

227.t: Buddy Rich's first band and Earl Swope
227.s: Mandel left Jimmy Dorsey for Buddy Rich's first band in 1946, a stiff band whose bright spot was trombonist Earl Swope, whom he compares to Carl Fontana.
227.ch: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
227.q: I was in three different bands, I was in that band until around June, about 6 months, it was the very first band Buddy ever had. It also was a stiff band, not a pleasant band to play in. A high priced stiff band. With good players, thank God, that was my first exposure to Earl Swope and he blew my…

227.t: Earl and Rob Swope and the Washington players
227.s: Mandel praises Earl Swope's time, says they became close, and talks about the Swope family and why the Washington musicians stayed home.
227.ch: Buddy Rich, Alvino Rey and Manhattan School
227.q: Yeah, Swope was a phenomenal trombone player, he had the same kind of time, probably the closest time, I could say he had was like Harry Edison’s time. It was that, you know, he didn’t need any rhythm section, he didn’t need anybody else. Sweets was like that, like a one man rhythm section, that’s…

137.t: How the trombone has been held back
137.s: Writers give trombones little; Durham says it has 14 positions, not seven, and wants to bring out more of what it can do.
137.q: Well, they always held the trombone back by trying to make an ________ instrument out of it, like a ________, which is supposed to tail along slow.

137.s: He wants to write for three B-flat trombones playing slurs, marking positions, and would try Dicky Wells.
137.q: trombones and that will show everybody what can be really played with a trombone. A trombone is made for slurring and movements. Nobody's ever written nothing for it that way. Move a little bit and that's the end of it, little bit . But if you ever heard a brass band and you heard that trombone,…

137.t: Trombone stylists: Dorsey, Wells, Higginbotham, Trummy Young
137.s: Asked who set trombone styles, Durham discusses Tommy Dorsey's sweet tone, Dicky Wells, J.C. Higginbotham and Trummy Young, who he thinks was buried.
137.q: Oh, well Tricky Sam was definitely one with the plunger and the moots was just a section (inaudible) of brass and the trombones have never did anything but just open trombone, just playing background.

137.t: Young trombonists who go too high
137.s: He and the interviewer say Bill Watrous and Phil Wilson go into the stratosphere, and nobody wants to play melody like Tommy Dorsey.
137.q: Yeah, maybe so. You got to watch that, too. They may not be able to go down to earth in there, but you got to get down to earth and whoever comes along now that can play like Tommy Dorsey will make history in the sweet song because nobody can play that tone like he played. I don't know whether you…

137.s: He played valve trombone on many Moten records; valves cut notes mechanically while slide players lip between positions, as in J.J. Johnson.
137.q: With Benny Moten, a lot of his records. That picture you looking at? That's a valve trombone there and a guitar. Nobody knows but that's a valve trombone sitting there in that '29 picture.

1.t: Cousin Big Belly Five-Ball, the comic trombonist
1.s: Danny remembers his relative Tapo, nicknamed Big Belly Five-Ball, who played trombone comically.
1.ch: A musical family and the old New Orleans bands
1.q: Tapo [SPELLS] His name was... I can't think of his last name, but... Yeah, it's Tapo. Yeah, that's right. Tapo. He played trombone, and he did it in a comic manner. He was big and fat. And his nickname was Big Belly Five-Ball. And he worked in the bands around. So you saw him.

1.t: Jim Robinson and Slow Drag, overrated by the revivalists
1.s: Danny says Jim Robinson's trombone pattern is repeated each chorus and the revival cult reveres him and bassist Slow Drag too much.
1.ch: A musical family and the old New Orleans bands
1.q: Jim Robinson was a trombone player who became...supposed to have been the greatest New Orleans trombone player after Kid Ory. Now, he was in that band. He was probably out to ...(?)... that band. But the Australian trombone players, they all got something from Jim Robinson -- which is the same…

1.t: The trombone players in the basement: Higginbotham, Herb Gregory, Wilson
1.s: Danny names the trombonists present that morning and notes Herb Gregory's skill, Herb Flemming being in Europe, and Wilson's challenges.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Higgenbotham. Herb Gregory. He was always starting something. Herb Gregory was a trombone player who could play. He was partly a boozer, but he was on time. But he had something about him. He drank so much that every time you spoke to him there was whiskey on his breath, see. So that annoyed some…

1.t: Big Green plays My Buddy as a waltz in a Seventh Avenue gin mill
1.s: Danny saw a down-and-out Big Green asked to play, and he improvised on a waltz that earned a standing ovation from other trombonists.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: No. That was where I saw Jabbo. All these people was in a gin mill on Seventh Avenue down in a basement, and I'm in there. And Big Green is in there, and he's drunk, and he'd lost his weight, and he said ain't nobody would hire him after Fletcher, and Chick Webb hired him for a while but he…

1.t: Charlie Johnson's band, Jimmy Harrison and the Harlem trombonists
1.s: Danny says Charlie Johnson's band at Small's rivaled Fletcher's, and he and Milt discuss Jimmy Harrison, Big Green and Stump.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: And In New York... He cut everybody in New York. Everybody who thought they could play a trumpet ain't messin'... Him and Jimmy Harrison, they were the two, trombone and trumpet... They were in Charlie Johnson's band, and they're speaking(?) to him, and then Sidney DeParis, and them three...…

614.t: Harris's solo Bijou and his original trombone sound
614.s: Herman picks Bijou, written for him by Ralph, as a masterpiece; Harris was widely imitated and sounded unlike Dorsey or Teagarden.
614.ch: The Second Herd and its sidemen
614.q: Yeah, well, I think he reached one of his high points, as far as the approach and the piece, the way it was written for him by Ralph, was 'Byou'. And I think it was a masterpiece what the way he played, it, as far as -- for the piece itself.

614.t: Jim Pugh, a meteoric trombone talent
614.s: Pugh first joined as second trombone, but when Bobby Burgess left in the early 1970s he was tried on lead and blossomed, staying over four years.
614.ch: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
614.q: Well, Jim Pugh as I think we've all learned has become one of the truly outstanding jazz musicians anywhere, in this day and age.

614.t: Herman's great trombonists and the shortage of trombone players
614.s: He lists Harris, Swope, Fontana, Urbie Green, Kai Winding and Frank Rehak, and agrees trombonists are scarce.
614.ch: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
614.q: And as a matter of fact, I've had probably one of the best arrays of trombone players of anyone who ever had a band. It started with Bill Harris and --

614.t: Eastman brass players: Pugh, Birch Johnson, Vizzutti
614.s: Eastman-trained brass players like Pugh, Birch Johnson and trumpeter Al Vizzutti share an approach; Vizzutti was sitting in with the band that night.
614.ch: Looking back, big bands and sidemen
614.q: Oh, I think he was very important and whenever it was possible we would utilize players from Eastman where he had studied, because they would have the same approach, general approach, to the way to play it and blow a trombone.

614.t: Harris and his trombone section buddies
614.s: Harris would demand better trombonists, then relent because they were his friends, and made them play far above themselves.
614.ch: The Second Herd and its sidemen
614.q: And he did something which I think was truly remarkable. I'd never witnessed this anywhere, ever, before or since. He took two very competent trombonists, but

297.t: Favorite trombonists Harrison Bradley and Boots Young
297.s: He took up trombone after seeing players, names Harrison Bradley and Albert 'Boots' Young as favorites, and says he sounds like Bradley and subbed for him in Kid Rena's band.
297.q: Well, we used to play on the same order. I mostly played my style. Where did you see him playing at then? Well, I used to be with him for all the time. When he was playing with Rene, he'd send me in his place when he couldn't go. Uh-huh. And you got to be good friends, I guess. Always good friends.…

297.t: Jack Teagarden and early trombone solos
297.s: Summers claims he and Jack Teagarden, who lived in New Orleans and played the Palace Theatre, were first to play trombone solos, ahead of Tommy Dawson; they studied with Gaspard together.
297.ch: Vic Gaspard and the Lyric Theatre
297.q: He used to play at the Palace Theatre. Yeah? Him and I was the first, Jack Teagarden, the first one started playing, uh, solos on trombone. Taking the lead.

297.t: Other trombonists: Harrison Bradley and the Young brothers
297.s: Summers names Bradley and Albert 'Boots' Young; Boots played with Bunk and Wooden Joe, and made high notes without teeth.
297.q: Let's call him Boots. Boots, yeah. That's Albert Young. That's Boots. He's called him Boots for nickname. Yeah. That's like Jim Crow. Yeah. Jam Robinson. I made some records with him playing the string bass with Wooden Joe Nicholas. Boots. Boots, yeah. He's a good trombone player too. Yeah, that's…

297.t: Vic Gaspard's playing at the Lyric Theater, his tone and instruments
297.s: Gaspard played Lyric Theater with John Robichaud, had a smooth tone, played slide trombone, baritone and bass horn, and was the oldest trombonist in town.
297.q: He played the baritone. He played the bass. The bass horn. The big tuba. The big tuba, yeah. He played all that. He didn't play the slide trombone? He played the slide trombone too. Oh he played the slide and the bass horn. Oh he played the slide then? Yes I know he played that. Slide, vowel, and…

8.s: Garland names Ory, Eddie Atkins, Honore Dutrey, George Fields and Eddie Vincent.
8.q: There you are again. Poor me, (unintelligible). So many of them I worked with a lot of good ones and a lot of bad ones. You know. I got to give all -- old Red the devil, which belongs to him. Ory, and I got to give Eddie Atkins, I got to give Honore Dutrey -- I'm calling trombone players. George…

8.t: Dandy Lewis, Frankie Duson and the Eagle Band
8.s: Bass player Dandy Lewis worked with Frankie Duson's very hot Eagle Band; Duson's trombone style compared with Jim Robinson; Willie Cornish's wife.
8.ch: Serenading and playing with Buddy Bolden
8.q: She used to live on Bertrand Street. No, Bolivar Street, I believe it was. Right around Tulane Avenue. You know where Tulane and Bolivar is? That neighborhood.

8.t: Jimmy Johnson and Don Albert's band
8.s: What became of bassist Jimmy Johnson, his travels with a band, and Garland hearing Don Albert's band on record.
8.ch: Bands and musicians around New Orleans
8.q: He was traveling, he traveled with, uh, his band, uh, Alvin Alcorn was working with. What was that by? So, uh, Bonnie Biggar's cousin or something like that.

8.t: Muggsy, Wild Bill Davison and the deParis brothers
8.s: He never worked with Muggsy Spanier or the deParis brothers but did with Wild Bill Davison.
8.q: Oh, my goodness, yeah, wild rascal.

881.t: Favorite trombone players and other musicians
881.s: Asked for favorites, he names J.J. Johnson and Kai Winding for bebop and Roy Palmer for old New Orleans, with Dickie Wells and others, plus brief talk of Oliver's eye.
881.q: Well if I had to pick a trombone player, these modern day trombone players, I'd have to pick them from the style. Now for that bebop, I like some of it, some of it I don't. But for the bebop, there's K. Wenge and there's J.J. Johnson, there's two best. I mean of the old times, your whole life, it's…

881.t: Vibrato, Dutre, Roy Palmer and Ory
881.s: He compares Dutre's smooth jazz solos with Roy's rough style, and rates Roy over Ory.
881.q: Well, to be truthful about the vibrato, I didn't pay any attention to the vibrato. You see, we'll just take Dutre for instance. Dutre and Zoo Robin was smooth. There was no one who played them shelly parts. And as you've heard Dutre when he played the jazz solos, his was a bit different than Roy.…

881.t: His trombone style compared with other trombonists
881.s: He says he never criticizes other trombonists, describes his range and mixed influences, and praises Vic Dickerson and Jack Teagarden.
881.q: Oh yeah, yeah. Up until recently. I had to. Well, no, I'm glad you asked this question. Now I'm supposed to play tonight. Now I've heard Louie Nelson.

881.s: Percy, a jazz trombonist whose last name he never knew.
881.ch: Learning trombone and the Wisconsin Roof years
881.q: Percy? Yeah. I mentioned Percy as trombones. Well you didn't say what he played. Yeah, he played trombones. But I never did know, and I never did know his last name. He was a good musician. He wasn't such a good musician. He could play well, but I mean as far as reading music. He was more of a jazz…

128.t: Best trombone players and playing with fast company
128.s: Robinson talks about trombonists in town and how playing with Harrison Bones and Chris Kelly's band improved him.
128.q: A real thunk trombone player, you know what I mean? Well, I tell you, at the time then, you see Dick, tell you the truth, them was more of a musical man, but good man, you understand? And they could play jazz too, you understand? But there was more musical man, you know? India was always good…

128.t: Other trombonists: Dude and Ernest Times
128.s: Allen asks about trombonists from Magnolia and Ernest Times, who played with the Claiborne Williams band.
128.q: No, no, not him, not him, not, uh-uh, uh-uh. Just another dude from Magnolia. With Magnolia, he's playing trombone. Yeah.

128.t: Eddie Morris, Zooey Sullen and Zooey Robinson
128.s: After Zooey Sullen was killed, Eddie Morris played trombone with Kid Punch; Zooey Robinson was another trombonist.
128.q: What about Eddie Morris? Who did he play with? Well, Eddie Morris, well after Zooey died, Zooey got killed, you know, but Eddie Morris went to a tram on with Kid Punch.

128.t: George Filhe, a good trombone player
128.s: Robinson says George Field played brass band and jazz and was a good trombonist.
128.q: He was playing brass band, and jazz band too. I think George was playing with only Robichaud I think. No, but I know what Vic Gasco, but Robichaud Trombone player. But I know George Field is one of them good bands.

677.t: The trombone section on his return
677.s: He names Booty Wood and Britt Woodman, Britt's trombonist father, and Butter Jackson.
677.ch: CBS, return to Ellington and retirement
677.q: Yes, that's possibly the right ones although there were quite a few changes after that. Booty, his wife, got ill, and he had to return home. And Britt he changed and he quit and he went into something else, and those kinds of things, you know.

677.t: Earlier trombone sections: Tizol, Tricky Sam, Claude Jones
677.s: He recalls Sandy Williams, Claude Jones, Wilbur De Paris and his own vacations.
677.ch: CBS, return to Ellington and retirement
677.q: Well, I would take vacations quite often, so I didn't -- I don't know who came in. And I really don't remember the exact times that I was out, but I would be out a month or so most every year.

677.s: Leon Cox, John Sanders, Benny Green as fourth trombone, and later men after he left in 1970.
677.ch: CBS, return to Ellington and retirement
677.q: Leon was in there a very short time. And see, there's many of them that would come in, stay a short few weeks and then go. So --

677.t: Feeling at home again and the bass trombone
677.s: His sound was a plus with Duke; the 1960s section was Chuck Connors and Buster Cooper, and bass trombone came into bands.
677.ch: CBS, return to Ellington and retirement
677.q: Well, the -- the bass trombone became prominent in all bands I remember just before I left CBS. They were looking for a bass trombone. And I -- that's the first time that I'd heard they were being played outside of symphonies.

256.t: Favorite trombone tone: Jerry Schrimmer and Murray McEachern
256.s: He names the finest tones he has heard, including his teacher.
256.q: Shimmer. He always, I got a picture of him there somewhere. He was about 80-some-odd. He was supposed to come down and see me.

256.s: Brief remarks on Shields, Schilling and trombonists on the coast.
256.q: Larry Shields. Wonderful. His brother plays good too down the road. This person was just here. They think that there's nobody like the Shields playing on it now with Chalky. Yeah, Harry is. She said she never liked Clarence, but she liked him.

256.t: His Tin Roof Blues trombone chorus
256.s: He played what felt natural; everyone copies it, including Wingy's Tijuana trombonist.
256.ch: New Orleans Rhythm Kings and Tin Roof Blues
256.q: No, we just played . Then we played . Then rap took that high chorus, and it was printed to me and I played . Just played what felt natural.

816.t: Sonny Henry on Jim and trombone styles
816.s: Sonny Henry talks about Jim, a trombonist friend he claims to have helped learn to talk, and compares players.
816.ch: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
816.q: Well what is he a real teen? Yeah. You see that's the thing I didn't know. I'm telling you right now back in those days I didn't know. All I'd know I used to just go to the dancers they could sit down there and play it. I wouldn't know if he was playing my head or not.

816.s: They run through trombonists of Warner's youth: Zue Robertson, Dutrey, Fields, Gaspard, Baptiste Delisle and Morris French.
816.q: I heard, uh, this fella, this young fella, yeah, he was, oh I can't think of that boy's name. He left, yeah, Zoo, Zoo Robertson. I was gonna ask you, just start asking, yeah, Zoo Robertson. Zoo Robertson? Well, he was a good friend of ours, you know. He was a good musician. Mm-hmm. Zoo Robertson,…

816.t: Sonny Henry on Jim, tailgate trombone who cannot read
816.s: Sonny Henry describes Jim as a strong tailgate man who never learned to read and only plays comfortably with his friends.
816.ch: Eureka Brass Band and Sonny Henry
816.q: Just like he said, he says, if Sonny is there or I'm there, he don't mind filling in for either one of us. Yeah, I've heard him get along pretty well. But if, he said, if either one of us ain't there, he said, he don't want to play.

14.t: Love's band and trombonist Buddy Brunson
14.s: Love begins talking about his boyhood band and describes Buddy Brunson, a tailgate valve-trombone player with a remarkable lip.
14.q: Williams' brother played the bass in the band and George Lewis. A fella in the name of Buddy Brunson. That man had the funniest lip I ever seen. I don't know what kind of trombone that he had. An E flat tenor trombone or something. A high one, a little one. Yeah. With the valve. With the valve. And…

14.t: Eddie Vinson's valve trombone and teacher George Williams; closing
14.s: Love says Vinson played valve trombone and could read, and mentions George Williams, a trick trombonist, before the interview ends.
14.q: At that time when I was practicing with him he played a valve trombone. But he could play that thing. He used to take a solo on it you know. Was he a good musician? Could he read and all? Yeah he could read right now. I hadn't started reading then when he was reading. I used to wish that I was…

14.s: Russell asks about Eddie Benson; Love says he first heard him practicing while working at the Navy Yard.
14.q: When I first met him, I was working at the Navy Yard and I used to hear them fellas practicing over there.

127.s: He praises trombonists Morris French and Earl Humphrey, then George Boyd, whom Allen notes Faulkner wrote about.
127.q: Well, he played on the style of aura, but he was so clean, you know. He made a little more stuff in aura in them days. Yeah, that's right. And Earl made more than any of them. Well, if they're trombone, I'd just be trumpet. Mm-hmm. Just like the guys playing now, we'll just play like that there.

127.t: Players with Jack Carey's trombone style
127.s: Eddie Morris and Morris French play like Carey; talk of Celestin's band.
127.ch: New Orleans halls and street bands
127.q: Well, ain't but one guy that seems like Eddie Morris, probably the only one. Cause all the rest of them, probably, they, uh, the way they play trombone now, they feel like they play trompones. Yeah, they all play in the lead. Yeah, but Eddie Morris got more, you know, that style, playing sides and…

127.t: Jimmy Blythe, Ed Ellis and who came before whom
127.s: Anecdotes about a trombonist's home town and the generations of New Orleans trumpeters.
127.q: I was wondering about somebody at that. Did you know Jimmy Blank, the piano player? Sure. I know him. But stuff says New York. So I asked him again, he says, tell him my home is in Philly. So he got sick, see. And he got really sick. Didn't nobody know what to do for everybody. So where was his…

831.t: Henry Fillmore pieces, brass bands, and Jack Teagarden as favorite
831.s: He never played Fillmore pieces or brass bands, and names Jack Teagarden as his favorite trombonist, soon to play the Dream Room.
831.ch: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
831.q: He's still top band for my mother. I'm gonna take you down there to see him.

831.t: Early New Orleans trombonists: Brunis, Gallaty, Ellibush, Perkins
831.s: He assesses the trombone players he knew, who played Dixieland and who read.
831.ch: Early bands and New Orleans musicians
831.q: No, not that I remembered of. The only one that I remember was Henny Brunus. He played fair trombone. He played fair trombone. And Bill Gallaty, well, he played vowel. He played a fair vowel trombone, see? And that's Joe Ellibusch, well, he was a horrible trombone player, but he... Like I tell you,…

831.t: Valve trombone, vamp style and trombone range in the early days
831.s: He discusses Bill Gallaty's valve trombone, his own vamp bass-part style, and the low range used, noting he never read music then.
831.q: No, no, not, not anymore than you could make it on a trumpet. Same, same as making it on a trumpet with the valve sliding up.

58.q: Morris French, Kid Ory, Jack Keran, and let's see who else I can... Who was with Buddy Petit? Morris French was with Rene. I'm trying to... Oh, yeah, a little boy, George Washington. He never did come back. Little bit of fella. Played nice trombone.

58.t: Sam Dutrey and trombonists Honore and Dick O'Hara
58.s: They sort out the Dutrey brothers and Miller recalls trombonists who played with him in Chicago.
58.q: Well, last time I seen Dutry was in Ohio. Mm-hmm. But he was still playing trombone. He was waiting in a club out there.

58.t: George Washington, Earl Humphrey and the fastest trombone players
58.s: Miller praises George Washington as a fast trombonist and says Earl Humphrey was a wizard; he does not know what became of Washington.
58.q: Oh, he was nice with a trombone player. For what? What kind of music? Oh, just swing stuff with jazz music. I don't think he was no good on them boxes or anything like that. Yeah.

574.t: Favourite trombonists and not playing with the marching bands
574.s: He did not play in the Tuxedo or Onward bands; admired Moise French and a trombonist with Clayton.
574.q: Yeah, I got a couple of young fellas under them, a little fella by the name of Moise French, used to play with Rene. I've heard of him, I never knew him. Yeah, I find he was a sweet little trombone player. We had another little fella that you played some nice trombone. He used to play with a little…

574.s: Frankie Duson, French, Earl Humphrey and others named.
574.q: didn't hear maybe did you ever hear carnage how was he whoa carnage well he wasn't anything special no make a whole lot of noise

574.t: Frankie Dusen and the trombone style of the day
574.s: Frankie Dusen inspired him to take up trombone; the harmony role of the trombone, valve versus slide.
574.q: Yeah, that's what got me stuck on the trombone by looking at Frankie Duesen. I was a little kid, but I used to like that. You liked that? I'd stare in under the band from the time to get there till the time to leave.

328.s: Many popular trombonists in the forties and fifties, from Tommy Dorsey to Lawrence Brown, all admired without a favorite.
328.q: There were many. At that time there were many trombone players that were very popular. Later in the fifties and sixties you started not to hear much of trombone players anymore. But in the forties and fifties there were a lot of trombone players that were popular. There was Tommy Dorsey, there was…

328.t: Origins of the World of Trombones; Al Grey
328.s: Trombone choirs, and why the group was formed, plus Al Grey.
328.ch: World of Trombones, family and institutions
328.q: The trombone choir had been something that’s existed for many years before we were even born, within the churches and in the classical ensembles. The choir has always been something that’s been important in music. So, usually, trombone players have a real camaraderie about them – among them. They…

328.s: Bobby Burgess's consistency and Bill Watrous.
328.ch: World of Trombones, family and institutions
328.q: Trombone players? It was Bobby Burgess. Bobby Burgess was with Stan Kenton, and then he was with Maynard. I played with him with Maynard. He was very consistent. There are guys that play higher than him, but there are not guys that are more consistent than he was.

69.t: Trombonists after Tricky Sam, and Britt Woodman
69.s: He can't name Tricky's replacement; Britt Woodman was a good first trombonist.
69.q: Oh, he was a good trombone player. I played with him with Nelson Riddle, and then Nat Cole and did a few recordings and with Duke Ellington, he was the first trombone player, and he was a good man. I liked him -- he did a lot of work around here.

69.t: Flamingo cues, Lawrence Brown's Stardust and the trombone section
69.s: He denies arranging Flamingo and praises Lawrence Brown; Duke said they had the best trombone section.
69.q: No, I don't arrange. I used to start it, you know? I would cue it and then the band would come in after that.

69.t: The Nelson Riddle band's trombones and length of work
69.s: Tommy Peterson played first trombone, Tizol third, with a bass trombonist whose name he forgets; they did a year of the show, plus one-nighters and recordings.
69.q: Well, I don't know. What's the name? Nelson Riddle would pick his band and keep them there all the time, like Tommy, the trombone player -- he was first trombone when I was there met-him; I was playing the third trombone.

173.t: Brass band trombones, Ricky Tom, Exchange Alley and the West End concert bands
173.s: Trombone players he knew, free-lunch beer in Exchange Alley, and Palletti's and Finney's concert bands of about fifty men playing at West End.
173.ch: American Brass Band and early bands
173.q: One? One. Just one. Now, of course, they had valve trombone or sliding trombone, and they had valve trombone. Now, Mr. Mallow from down below, his brother used to be a valve trombone player. But he was good, but he never read nothing. But he had a good ear. You could take that fella and you played…

173.t: Fisher, Brunus and other uptown players; the Lane neighbor
173.s: He doesn't know Fisher, Schilling or Tom Brown; he mentions a neighbor Lane and a deceased brother who played trombone.
173.q: He's working out there on Tulane Avenue in that big uh uh uh St. Clair and there's three of them mixed up in that big factory they think. They fixed up machinery and patron makers I think and so on. Yeah, the patron makers. Well that's where he was and that's that's his son I'll tell you about.

868.t: Role of the trombone and old-time trombone soloists
868.s: Trombone 'tore paper' with long slide notes in the old days; Willie Cornish is named as someone who took many solos.
868.q: In other words he'd be tearing paper just making those long notes, you know, we call that tearing paper, you know. Ta, ta. They'd take those hearts like they take today now. And the trombone players play almost like a trumpet player today, make all those variations today, you know. At that time…

868.t: Favorite old trombone players: Sonny Henry, Joe Petit, Showboy
868.s: De De names trombonists he liked, including the Petit brothers and Showboy Thomas.
868.q: Well, like I said, Sonny, I remember how he was. I remember the brothers, several of them, before my time.

859.t: Jimmy Strode, old man Barbarin and the DuPas brothers
859.s: Brief remarks on Jimmy Strode, Barbarin, and Dave and Rudolph DuPas.
859.ch: Trumpet players of the old days
859.q: Well, he was a fellow who used to play that trumpet, and he had all them got beats about him. Old man Barbara, you heard him, I'll have to tell you about him. I know you're old boy. He was a nice musician too.

859.t: Sugar Johnny, Roy Palmer, Harrison Ball and Sam Baldwin
859.s: Gabriel describes trumpeters Sugar Johnny, Roy Palmer, Harrison Ball, and Sam Baldwin's band.
859.ch: Trumpet players of the old days
859.q: He was a good trumpet player. Yeah, I've heard about him. I played in the band with him too, drummer. I don't play in the band with Sugar Johnny. Sugar Johnny was a nice trumpet player. He played with Roy Palmer.

179.t: Buddy Johnson, Yank Johnson and Harrison Bones
179.s: Great trombonists Buddy Johnson and Harrison Bones, who came from downriver, switched from trumpet, and had a stroke.
179.q: Well, I guess you might have known, uh, probably you might have known, uh, Buddy Johnson and Yang Johnson? No, that was before my time.

179.t: Good trombone players who played by head
179.s: Yank, Papa Petit, Carnish and Frankie Dusen as head trombonists; Yank began on valve trombone.
179.q: what I know the uh I believe Yank was about the honest one I know at that time at my time that played trombone by head and uh old man Petit I played buddy Petit there old man Petit he played I think he played by head because John used to call him Papa Petit all the time he had no teeth in his mouth…

826.t: John Pendleton, Claymore Williams and David Jones in California
826.s: They talk of John Pendleton, Claymore Williams and his brother the baritone player, and trying to find David Jones in California.
826.q: Yeah, and his brother... Tell me his brother was one of the greatest biotone players. It was George. George, that's right.

826.s: Willie J. recalls Lewis Dumaine from the WPA band and recordings, and trombonist Gus Metcalf, a cousin of Bob Lyons taught by the grandfather.
826.q: Oh, that's right. The Red Onion Drag. And this Ann Cookie here I'm talking about. Oh, yeah, that's right. He made something. He certainly did.

634.t: The Eagle band and trombonist Frankie Dusen
634.s: The Eagle band was a dance band led by Frankie Dusen, whom he first heard playing valve trombone when he was about 15 or 16; he describes his playing.
634.q: No, I never did know him to play with. It's the only one, the only one I know played Val Trambo and was... Harnished.

634.s: Sonny Allen, Albert Russo, Bill Madden and Buddy Johnson were good trombone soloists.
634.q: Yeah. Place the second. First and second together. That's pretty. It is. When they play together. Yeah. Right. 51 is good for that. 51, they really good number.

773.t: Pops and Willie Foster, and Kid Ory's band
773.s: The Fosters, and a trombone player with a brass band.

773.t: Guzi and Zoo Robertson; everyone was a musician
773.s: She recognizes some names and says everyone then was a musician; singing on Kings Day.
773.q: He was so much musicians. Oh, yeah. There used to be plenty them days. They don't be, look like the posts they have, but you don't hear musicians like them, do you? Look like everybody you knew them days was a musicians. Most everybody look like you knew of, you know. Yeah. Everybody wanted to play…

22.t: New trombonist replaces Edwards, and unreleased records
22.s: He explains how Emil learned Edwards's parts after Edwards was drafted and mentions two unreleased Victor records.
22.q: Oh, yes. Edwards was drafted around, in the middle, almost in fall. We came to New Orleans to get a trombone player. Emil played connet. He had been with several bands up to Chicago. And they were unsuccessful. He came back to New Orleans to play. And when we came back here to look for a trombone…

22.t: Edwards on trombone, borrowed chords, and the band's new rhythm

453.s: The 1933 band had more sideman solos; Randolph praises Budd Johnson on tenor and Keg Johnson's lip-trilling trombone.
453.q: Yes, that's right. Budd Johnson was a good tenor man, and Keg was a good -- those two Johnson boys, like, Budd (unintelligible), I mean, Keg is dead now.

117.t: Hearing Jack Teagarden in a speakeasy
117.s: While in Pollack's band Freeman hears Teagarden play alone in a speakeasy, and Pollack hires him after one chorus.
117.q: No, I want to say particularly if I may, that I have tremendous respect for Jack Teagarden and there was a story about him that -- I remember that I was playing with the Pollack band, in New York, and Glenn Miller had given his notice and so Ben said & well, we will be looking for another trombone…

29.t: Happy Johnson, Andy Anderson and Bob Dorsey
29.s: Collette fishes for names; Howard recalls Happy Johnson as a Texas trombonist and Bob Dorsey as a good tenor player, but few details.
29.ch: The union and the 1920s-30s band scene
29.q: Happy. I can remember, a lot of things I can't remember about those fellows, but I know them all.

99.t: Gus Wilson, trombonist and arranger, Teddy Wilson's brother
99.s: A gifted but troubled trombonist and arranger who walked off if complimented, left for his mother's in Des Moines and died soon after.
99.q: In later years when the band started kind of disintegrating a little bit, we picked up a guy named Gus Wilson. Gus Wilson was the brother of Teddy Wilson. Gus Wilson was a genius. But it seems as though in the family his father had always thrown up Teddy to Gus -- "Why don't you be like Teddy?" And…

148.t: The trombonist and bass trumpeter who left for New York
148.s: Handy praises a trombonist, probably Johnny Mandel, who left to join the bebop movement.
148.q: He played trombone on Boyd's band, but I think when he played with Basie I have an idea that he may have been playing bass trumpet.

611.t: Rollini, Bix and the three-trombone battle at Small's Paradise
611.s: Waters was most struck by Rollini's bass saxophone and Bix, and recalls a battle of Miff Mole, Jack Teagarden and Jimmy Harrison at Small's, which Harrison won. He later got a bass saxophone in California.
611.q: And the one who knocked me out the most as a saxophone player, see - I didn't hear any tenor players at that period that knocked me out more than Coleman, you understand what I mean, I didn't hear any - but that guy on the bass, Rollini, on the bass saxophone, every note he made was great. And…

19.t: J.J. Johnson's trombone concept in the Jacquet band
19.s: Johnson plays fast, articulate lines with a short slide, drawing questions from symphony players.
19.ch: Trio, Eckstine accompanist and Illinois Jacquet, 1945-48
19.q: Oh, I forgot to mention the other person in the band that was very significant. I don't know how I missed him. It was J.J. Johnson. I kept thinking back, counting the people that I named. I named Leo Parker and Illinois, of course, and Joe Newman, and Illinois' brother, Russell, and of course, the…

428.t: Teddy Wilson band sections and Hall's lack of road experience
428.s: Shorty Baker, other brass and reeds, trombonist Jake Wiley and teacher Bobby Burns, and Hall never having travelled.
428.ch: Teddy Wilson bands and Cafe Society
428.q: Because he sounds so pretty. He's a beautiful person. He was the backbone of the trumpet section and then we had Doc Cheatham, Karl George and , well, I already mentioned the reed section.

389.t: Tommy Dorsey quits and Bill Rank replaces him
389.s: Tommy decided to leave in Chicago; Challis recruited Bill Rank, and Tommy impressed the band playing Louis Armstrong choruses on a small trumpet.
389.q: It turned out good and so did the other record, the Washboard and that and I was off to a good start, so in the meantime I'm working out a couple arrangements with like Tommy and Jimmy, trying to get them set in what they like to do. One night out in Chicago, we played three different theatres in…

413.t: Trummy Young in Honolulu and his influence on trombone playing
413.s: In Honolulu, Trummy Young asks about the system; Maxwell calls Trummy the father of modern trombone playing.
413.q: : Tommy was very impressed with my chops. He said, man -- you know, he kept raving about my range and endurance and my age and everything.
